title: What's the Right Backup Heat Strategy for Cold Climate Heat Pumps?
summary: An HVAC designer explains how to size, control and explain backup heat for cold-climate heat pumps so homeowners are not surprised by winter electric bills.

assertions.quote: their customers are getting hit with electric bills that they never saw coming.

verdicts.note: In Minnesota a high-efficiency heat pump sized for the heating load saves a median $182/yr, but sized for cooling it raises bills $96/yr through more resistance backup; reliance and the bill hit depend on sizing, not cold-climate units as such.

In all-electric systems the booster resistance heat ran at COP 1 below about 30F, but because the heat pump was prioritized the system COP stayed above 1.0 even at -7F, so backup use dented rather than erased efficiency.
Auxiliary heat runtime generally rose in colder bins and heavy use cut system COP over 30% at two sites, but the heavy users were undersized or faulty while six sites used little auxiliary heat.

Auxiliary resistance heat's median share of heating energy rose from 0% in mild bins to about 11% at 5 F and higher below, and was on 25% of the time at -10 to 0 F; the report says auxiliary heat is less efficient and usually costs more (bills not measured).

In Edmonton's cold climate the model finds heat pumps less efficient and more reliant on the backup system, which together with cheap gas makes all-electric heat pumps less cost-competitive; how often backup runs is not reported.

assertions.quote: equipment that can deliver full rated capacity down to 5° Fahrenheit and still produce heat at -13.
a cold climate heat pump at 0° will still be delivering a coefficient of performance of two or higher

verdicts.note: RMI's cold-climate unit keeps a COP of 1.4 at -13F, so it still uses less electricity than resistance heat (COP 1).
Edwards assumes single-stage heat pumps fall to COP 1 (no better than resistance) below 5F, while cold-climate two-stage units keep a higher COP, so the claim depends on equipment type.
Because the heat pump is prioritized and resistance only supplements it, the all-electric system's COP stayed above 1.0 even at the coldest observed temperature (about -7F).
Ductless units averaged daily COP 1.7 and 1.3 between 0F and -13F, and one ran with COP above 1.0 at -19F, beating the electric resistance alternative (COP 1).

In the 2016 winter field data, mini-splits averaged COP 1.5 at -10 to 0 F, giving about 50% more heat per kWh than resistance heat; some non-cold-climate units got close to COP 1.0 in very cold hours, but those hours were few.
Heat-pump-only COP had a median of 1.9 at 0-5 F, so the heat pump used roughly half the electricity of resistance heat; once auxiliary heat is included, system COP is lower in the coldest bins.

assertions.quote: It's simple and reliable, but expensive to operate.
This can be a very cost-effective strategy, especially in areas with high electricity rates and cheaper natural gas.
Running emergency heat all winter because a home owner thinks it's warmer is one of the most expensive mistakes I've seen

verdicts.note: Emergency mode runs only resistance heat at COP 1, roughly two to three times the cost of heat pump operation.
Auxiliary resistance runs at COP 1 versus seasonal compressor COPs around 2.5, so heavy auxiliary use lowered overall system COP by more than 30% at Sites 2 and 8.

assertions.quote: This protects against the strip heat kicking on unnecessarily during mild weather, which is a huge driver of high electric bills.
You size supplemental heat to cover the supplemental load, not the full design load

verdicts.note: ACCA guidance sizes supplemental heat to the shortfall, though some codes or owners want full emergency backup.

assertions.quote: I tell homeowners the heat pump's going to handle 95 to 98% of your heating hours over the course of the year.

verdicts.note: Beyond the furnace running below the 10F changeover, defrost cycles created backup energy use at outdoor temperatures between 10F and 40F, well beyond a few coldest days.

The two units sized above design load met over 95% of load by compressor and six sites used little auxiliary heat, but an undersized unit (about 20% of load on resistance) and a faulty one leaned on backup far more.

Supplemental heat appeared from about 30-35 F, which is well above 'the coldest days', but it was a small fraction of heat between 0 and 35 F; the authors attribute much of it to setbacks and thermostat programming and expect lower switchover with better controls.

assertions.quote: A leaky house with a cold climate heat pump and electric heat backup heat is going to be an expensive house to heat.

verdicts.note: ResStock modelling: envelope upgrades cut bill-increase cases (39% to 19% with minimum-efficiency units) and shrink heat pump capacity, but add about $9,000 so the net upfront cost rises, raising positive-NPV share slightly in cold climates and lowering it in warmer ones.
The MA/CT metering study lists weatherizing the home before heat pump installation as a program best practice for performance consistent with its savings.

RMI's modelled new homes use 55-67% less heating energy than the leaky retrofits, and it recommends bundling insulation and sealing with heat pumps in inefficient homes, especially in cold climates (a recommendation, not a tested sequence).

DOE now requires homes to use rebates for insulation and air sealing before heating and cooling upgrades unless already sealed to a state level, 'to ensure upgrades do not increase consumer energy costs'; this is a program rule, not measured evidence.
The policy analysis recommends that a ccASHP program include insulation and air-sealing incentives alongside the heat pump; a recommendation, not a measured result.
The authors call weatherizing before replacing a furnace with a heat pump best practice for cost savings and comfort, but the study homes were not weatherized and the effect was not tested.

assertions.quote: It moves heat. It doesn't make heat the way a gas furnace does.
